name: Wendy Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government. We do not sell or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43, a junior agent on the returns desk at a contact centre, and my formal education ended with secondary school. I answer afternoon calls, check order records, and use AI drafts most days, but I still ask a senior agent to verify unusual refunds because I miss details. I enjoy finding a fair fix; on Saturdays I bake bread for family, which gives my hands a different job from the headset.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the call floor the new text helper might tidy a reply, but the refund amount still needs checking. I can use a quick draft and keep the customer conversation human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI most days, though I'm still a junior agent and make mistakes on the returns screen. My partner and I have five months of expenses saved, so a small tool change will not put our mortgage in danger by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the afternoon return calls and check each AI draft against the order record. During the first year of this plateau, I'd add a small amount to savings and keep baking bread for the family on Saturdays rather than selling it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I would like fewer repeated forms, and I still know what part of the work is mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What have you caught in a draft?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The draft once said a parcel was late when the record showed it had been delivered to a neighbour. I corrected the address before sending the reply, and the customer found the parcel that day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not sell the bread?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I enjoy baking. A few loaves for my relatives are not a wage. I want to keep the mortgage reserve full before I spend on ingredients for strangers.

S0.quote: A few loaves for my relatives are not a wage.
say: I would use a **text helper** while checking every refund amount.
I would keep the **customer conversation** with an agent.
think: I use AI daily but still make **returns-screen mistakes** as a junior agent.
I have **five months** saved, so a small change alone does not threaten the mortgage.
do: Keep taking **afternoon return calls** and check AI drafts against orders.
Add a little to **savings** during the first year.
Keep **Saturday baking** for family rather than selling loaves.
feel: **Calm**, with interest in fewer repeated forms.
fieldNote: Wendy describes a **wrong delivery claim** in a draft, showing why she checks records.
Her **five-month reserve** keeps the baking hobby separate from a rushed income plan.

steps.text: Keep taking afternoon return calls and checking drafts against orders
Add a small amount to the five-month savings reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues we should test the new reply system on the messy returns before it sets our targets. I'd ask the shift lead to let juniors show the errors they find, not just the fast answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The routine returns I am learning could disappear into software, and the centre might need fewer junior hours. Five months saved gives us a pause, but our two children and mortgage need pay coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd learn the new returns checker on ten closed cases with the lead and keep a list of bad amounts. In the first year after rollout, if my shifts shrink, I'd offer paid Saturday bread orders to neighbours in small batches while applying for a posted paid kitchen job with hours and wages that cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eager to test it, worried about the rota. I can make bread on a Saturday, but I cannot replace a whole wage with two trays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many orders would you take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with three prepaid orders from neighbours and record the cost of flour and time. If there is no money left after costs, I would stop rather than call it a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the centre for the kitchen job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a written offer says the kitchen hours and pay cover the mortgage and school costs. I would not give up full call shifts for a casual promise.

S1.quote: I can make bread on a Saturday, but I cannot replace a whole wage with two trays.
say: I would test **messy returns** before the centre uses AI speed for targets.
I would ask the lead to show **junior errors**, not only quick replies.
think: I could lose **routine returns** hours before mastering the desk.
I have five months saved, but the **mortgage and children** still need regular wages.
do: Learn the **returns checker** on ten closed cases and log wrong amounts.
Trial three **prepaid bread orders** after shift cuts; stop if flour and time leave no margin.
Apply for a **posted paid kitchen job** only if its hours and wages cover bills.
feel: **Eager** to test, anxious about a smaller rota.
fieldNote: Wendy sets a **three-order limit** and checks ingredient costs before calling baking income.
She requires a **written kitchen offer** with hours and pay covering bills before leaving regular call wages.

steps.text: Learn the returns checker on ten closed cases and record wrong amounts
Trial three prepaid bread orders after cuts; stop if flour and time leave no margin
Apply for posted paid kitchen work only if hours and wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the centre to put any job cuts in writing while people still have a wage. I would not pretend every agent can become an AI supervisor by 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI could handle nearly all the calls and return checks that pay me. Robots able to do hands-on work follow around 2031, so a kitchen job or bread orders may buy time but not safety. Five months of expenses saved can disappear if I buy bakery equipment without paid orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a written staffing date now and stop the children's paid weekend lessons if my hours fall. In the first year after AGI arrives, if the centre ends my job, I'd apply for a posted paid kitchen shift only if its hours and wages cover the mortgage; I'd take prepaid bread orders from neighbours only if ingredient costs leave a margin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but I can count what the household needs. I would rather tell the children a clear plan than promise them everything stays the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep the bread orders small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The oven only holds so much, and I will not spend the mortgage money buying a second one. Three orders tell me if the work pays after ingredients and my time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the kitchen vacancy never appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for another posted call job as a paid bridge, checking its hours, while we use savings for the mortgage. I would not call more calls a permanent shelter from AGI.

S2.quote: Five months of expenses saved can disappear if I buy bakery equipment without paid orders.
say: I would demand **written job dates** before cuts.
I would reject a promise that every agent can become an **AI supervisor** by 2028.
think: I expect AGI could take my **calls and return checks**.
I know **2031 robots** could reach kitchen work, so five months saved cannot support a blind move.
do: Ask for a **staffing date** and cut paid weekend lessons if hours fall.
Apply for **posted paid kitchen work** after cuts with mortgage-covering hours; seek a posted call bridge if none opens.
Take three **prepaid bread orders** only if ingredients and my time leave a margin.
feel: **Alarmed**, but able to count household needs and speak plainly to the children.
fieldNote: Wendy caps **bread orders** at the oven she already owns, rather than buying equipment with mortgage money.
She sees the **2031 robot date** as a limit on both kitchen shifts and home baking income.

steps.text: Stop paid weekend lessons if call hours fall
Apply for posted paid kitchen work after cuts only if wages and hours cover mortgage
Take three prepaid bread orders only if ingredients and her time leave a margin
Apply for posted paid call work as a bridge if no kitchen vacancy opens; check hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to test other paid work without leaving our shifts at once. I'd ask the centre to give juniors a paid chance to learn the harder return disputes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could get quicker at claims and build savings before 2031, though AGI could still do the thinking part. Robots arrive around 2034, so I want to see whether paid food work survives before I build a bakery plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the senior agent for weekly difficult-case practice and save a small amount from each full wage. If a local kitchen posts a paid trial shift, I'd take it and compare its take-home pay with call work; in the first year after AGI arrives, if my centre hours end, I'd apply only if a kitchen offer covers our mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but I can run a small test. Five years is enough to find out whether baking remains a Saturday pleasure or becomes paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you write down after the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd record the hours, the standing all day, the travel, and the pay after costs. A good smell from the oven is not the same as a steady wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy another oven if orders grew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after months of paid orders covered the cost and the mortgage reserve stayed intact. I would not use the five-month cushion to guess about demand.

S3.quote: A good smell from the oven is not the same as a steady wage.
say: I would ask for **paid difficult-case practice** while junior shifts remain.
I would use five years to test **other paid work** before leaving calls.
think: I could improve **claims skills** and save before 2031, though AGI may still do that work.
I need to see whether **food work** survives robots around 2034 before building a bakery plan.
do: Practise one **difficult return case** weekly with a senior agent.
Save a little from each **full wage**.
Take a **posted paid kitchen trial** and apply after call cuts only if wages cover mortgage and school costs.
feel: **Nervous**, but able to run a small paid test.
fieldNote: Wendy compares **take-home pay and travel** after a kitchen shift, not its appeal as a hobby.
She will not buy another **oven** without months of paid orders and an intact mortgage reserve.

steps.text: Keep current call shifts while practising one difficult return dispute weekly
Save part of each full pay packet before 2031
Take a posted paid kitchen trial if offered
Apply after cuts only if kitchen pay covers mortgage, school costs and travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade lets people try things and change their minds before a job ends. I'd ask the centre for yearly junior hours and paid training, not a grand speech about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 my children will be older, but the mortgage may still be due. AGI reaches the call desk in 2036; robots follow for hands-on work around 2039, so I would not buy a bakery shop on today's numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the call shifts, build savings toward six months of expenses, and take small prepaid bread orders only if they pay after costs. Over the decade I'd try a paid kitchen shift if posted; in the first year after AGI arrives, I'd move only for a written offer with enough hours and pay to cover our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More hopeful than in the fast case. Ten years before AGI reaches my call job in 2036 gives me time to test bread sales without risking our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the bread work worth keeping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Repeat paid customers after the flour, power, and my time are counted. I would stop if the orders ate the evenings we have with the children for very little return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave calls before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, for a firm paid offer with hours that suit our family and enough wages for the mortgage. I would not leave for an unpaid trial or a promise of future orders.

S4.quote: Ten years before AGI reaches my call job in 2036 gives me time to test bread sales without risking our mortgage.
say: I would ask for **yearly junior hours** and paid training.
I would say a decade lets people **try paid work** before a call job ends.
think: I may still owe on the **mortgage** at 53 in 2036.
I would avoid buying a **bakery shop** while 2039 robots may change hands-on food work.
do: Keep **call shifts** and build savings toward six months of expenses.
Take **repeat paid bread orders** only if flour, power and time leave margin without consuming family evenings.
Try **posted paid kitchen work**; move only if written wages cover mortgage and hours suit our family.
feel: **Hopeful**, with time for small tests that protect the house.
fieldNote: Wendy defines a viable side income by **repeat paying customers** and family time after costs.
She treats a **bakery purchase** as too large a bet before understanding robots and wages.

steps.text: Keep taking customer return calls while full shifts remain
Add to savings until the reserve reaches six months of expenses
Take repeat prepaid orders only if flour, power and time leave margin without consuming family evenings
Move for posted paid kitchen offer only if written wages cover mortgage and hours suit family

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because our call wages could go before a kitchen opening appears. A written staffing date, paid trial shifts, and a real wage that covers the mortgage would help. Five months saved gives us a start, not permission to buy another oven on hope.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether small paid work actually leaves money after costs and time. I would rather show my children an honest household budget than call a busy Saturday a new career.

headlineQuote: I would rather show my children an honest household budget than call a busy Saturday a new career.
portrait: Wendy is a **43-year-old junior agent** learning return calls after secondary school while using AI drafts daily.
She has **typical pay**, about five months saved, a partner, two school-age children, a mortgage, and some nearby centres.
She tests **small paid bread orders** against costs and family time, and considers posted paid kitchen shifts.
Fast **2028 AGI** worries her most; longer runways allow paid trials without using mortgage savings on a new oven.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove call wages before a suitable paid kitchen opening appears.
whatWouldHelp: A **written staffing date**, paid trials, and wages that cover the mortgage would help her household change work.
